James Hopkins The late Sandra Day O’Connor, the first woman to serve on the United States Supreme Court, once said “Those who would renegotiate the boundaries between church and state must therefore answer a difficult question: why would we trade a system that has served us so well for one that has served others so poorly.?” With these words Justice O’Connor states succinctly the challenge before us. Religious nationalisms, like other nationalisms, are not a new thing in human history. Their force and power have waxed, as they have waned, but the idea that the adherents of a particular theology, wrapped into the apparatus of a particular political philosophy, should have authority over all they come into contact with, has been tried repeatedly, and repeatedly found wanting. Why she asks, why would we trade something that has been proven to work, democracy, for something that has been proven not to work, religious nationalism? Look at what is going on in our world today. Is Islamic nationalism working? Is Buddhist nationalism working? Is Jewish nationalism working? Is white Christian nationalism working? Democracy is a system of governance in which power is vested in the people, who exercise that power directly through the vote and indirectly through elected representatives. It is characterized by principles such as political equality, free and fair elections, the rule of law, and the protection of individual rights and freedoms. In a democratic society, citizens have the right to participate in decision-making processes and to hold their leaders accountable. So defined, democracy works, albeit imperfectly, much better than any system of religious nationalism has ever worked. Thus, my main point, Christian nationalism threatens democracy by trying to replace something that has been proven to work, democracy, with something that has been proven not to work, Christian nationalism; something superior with something inferior. articles.text: The Piedmont League of Women Voters hosted a virtual candidates forum for the East Bay Regional Park District Ward 2 election. A recording of the forum is now available on the League’s YouTube channel at https://www. youtube.com/watch?v=2vVlUWyWJ4E The forum was moderated by Piedmont League member Jennifer Nixon and was co-sponsored by the Oakland and West Contra Costa County Leagues. Candidates Lynda Deschambault, Casey Farmer and Shane Reisman participated. The candidates addressed a number of issues, including public safety, fire safety, accessible transportation, and climate change. Questions were pre-selected from among those submitted by community members and reviewed by a group of LWVP members. Ballots for the November election were mailed on October 7. Voters may cast their ballots in person or by mail. For those voting absentee an official Alameda County ballot drop box is at the corner of Highland Way and Mountain Avenue in Piedmont. You can register to vote online through October 21, 2024, by 5pm. Same day registration is available in person through election day, November 5, 2024. Please remember to vote on or before November 5, 2024.

articles.text: Vote YES on Measure P: Keep our schools, property values strong Editor: As a Piedmont graduate who returned to raise my family here, I know how important our schools are – not only for students, but for our pocketbooks, too. Whether or not you have children enrolled, our schools are working for you by keeping demand for homes high and protecting property values. Investing in our schools through Measure P is an investment in your home’s value. That is why I am voting Yes on Measure P. Measure P is an essential parcel tax that will provide funds for attracting and retaining high-quality teachers and offering advanced programs. This commitment to excellence will continue to draw families to Piedmont, ensuring a vibrant housing market that benefits all homeowners. Voting Yes on Measure P is necessary for our teachers, the long-term health of our community, and our home values. Our community stands out for its willingness to support our schools through a long tradition of parcel taxes and private donations. Piedmont residents have passed previous versions of this critical parcel tax nine times over the years, helping to keep our schools strong. Strong schools mean strong property values — it’s that simple. Please join me in voting Yes on Measure P. –Amelie Kappes mont City Council. –Betsy Smegal Andersen Vice Mayor, City of Piedmont While those of us who have kids currently in the Piedmont public education system clearly benefit from support to the schools, we must all remember that our entire community centers around public education. Our incredible schools are the backbone of our community and are essential to making Piedmont so special. We must all bear in mind that our schools will remain incredible only if we all invest in them. We urge our fellow Piedmonters to support our teachers, our schools, and each other with this manageable, essential contribution. Join us in voting Yes for Measure P. –Matthew Zapruder and Sarah Karlinsky

articles.text: Editor: In response to a letter by Michael Gallagher regarding plans to convert the Shell Station to an electric vehicle charging center. I had no idea that the proposed equipment would generate such a powerful electromagnetic field and that it would be a health risk to humans. Your attachments and references certainly provide corroboration for your statements about the risk. Putting this equipment in an underground vault near the intersection of Grand and Wildwood Avenues would certainly seem to be the safest location for this equipment on the site, that is if it is safe to even have it there. It is very disappointing that the consultants from LSA who prepared the IS/ MND were seemingly unaware of this significant environmental impact. I’m glad that you made your comments on the IS/MND and I look forward to reading the next draft of the IS/MND to see how they address this issue. –Malcolm Talcott
articles.title: Concerns about removal of Shell Station

articles.text: The public is invited to St, Paul’s Episcopal Church in Oakland for a special viewing of the film A Case for Love on Saturday, November 2, at 2:00 p.m. The heartfelt, personally challenging movie inspired by the teachings and writings of Presiding Bishop Michael Curry, most well-known for his passionate sermon about “The Power of Love” at the royal wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle. This film examines whether or not love – specifically unselfish love – is the solution to the extreme societal and political divide facing the U.S. In the documentary, the cinematographers travel across the country interviewing everyday people from various walks of life and ethnicities. Stories include racial justice, the military, foster care, sexual trafficking, love and loss and others as well-known figures including Pete Buttigieg, Al Roker, Sam Waterston, Becca Stevens, Russell Moore, John Danforth, John Clyburn, Kelly Brown Douglas, and Jon Meacham weigh in on the issue. Ultimately, Bishop Michael Curry puts what we’ve seen into context. What’s the verdict on “ A Case for Love?” Come watch and decide for yourself. A Q&A led by film director Brian Ide and the Rev. Dr. Mauricio Wilson, St. Paul’s rector will follow the screening. For a preview, watch the film’s trailer at https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=jLTxUBCbLiQ. St. Paul’s Episcopal Church is located at 114 Montecito Avenue in Oakland.

articles.text: Astropoet John Fang presents his work publicly On September 21, local poet John Fang (Chinese name Fang Xin 方莘) presented his poetry at the Piedmont home of Deede Liu and Dan Aires. As a student in Taiwan 55 years ago, Fang had already been recognized and received awards as a leading poet. More recently, with the encouragement of his daughter Etienne Fang, and assistance from Berkeley poet David Roderick, John began translating his original Chinese work into English. He is a rare poet who is able to compose in both his native language and his adopted language. The assembled friends, family, and admirers were treated to a reading of 11 poems including his “Horsehead Nebula,” which refers to the classic characters of Homer’s Iliad. It includes recent WWII history and a contemporary tragedy in America, to draw connections and reveal historical patterns. Sprinkled throughout the poem are allusions to astronomical objects which John is fond of tracking at the Chabot Observatory, where he serves as Archivist. He is also a member of the Eastbay Astronomical Society, hence his “Astropoet” moniker. Fang Xin derives inspiration from music, especially the sounds of Chopin from which he composed four poetic Études. He has been collaborating with Holly Mead, a pianist, composer, and Bilingual poet, translator, star-gazer, and Piedmont resident, Fang Xin, reading his most recent poem, “Horsehead Nebula” David Roderick (left) of Left Margin Lit in Berkeley, the writing adviser to Fang Xin Holly Mead and artist Onikho describing the unique arrangement of “Night falls so impatiently” recording artist, who composed melodies to accompany the spoken words. Holly was joined by singer and composer Carina Ho (Onikho). Together, they took the combination of music and poetry to new experiences as their two voices echoed and re-echoed words and phrases while the poet’s voice slowly unfurled the stanzas. The stanzas are laid out on the page in a way that suggests a musical score. Usually shy and self-effacing, John’s personal presentation of his poetry was warmly appreciated. “I exposed myself to the Universe,” Fang confessed, as the Universe who heard him applauded. Fang Xin’s poems were recently published in the New England Review (volume 44.3, 2023) and the Georgia Review (Summer 2023). Fang Xin will be having a Chinese rendition of this event in Taipei, Taiwan, on October 30th, at National Taiwan University with Holly Mead, performing his own poetry in Chinese. articles.text: A long-standing Halloween tradition continues this Saturday, October 26, from 12 p.m. to 3 p.m., with Mountain View Cemetery’s 16th annual Pumpkin Festival. The free event follows the Piedmont Avenue Merchants Association’s annual Halloween Parade, which is part of a daylong celebration that includes trick-ortreating at businesses all along the avenue. “The parade is a much longer tradition, but we decided to put on this festival at the coattails of the event 16 years ago so the tricks and treats would continue through the day,” said Kristie Ly, special events coordinator for the cemetery. At the festival, parent- or guardian-accompanied children can choose a free pumpkin from a broad, festive patch and enjoy activities including several inflatable bounce houses; a hay bale tunnel; treat tents with free candy bags; a clown balloon artist; face painters; an area with arts and crafts tents to decorate pumpkins, masks and treat bags; and food truck vendors selling tacos, empanadas, Chinese bao burgers, cupcakes, smoothies and shaved ice. The event will also feature live jazz, blues and swing music by Pumpkins and hay bales will await Pumpkin Festival-goers at Mountain View Cemetery this Saturday following the Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade. the locally based Donna Spitzer Jazz Group. “Other than the food trucks, the event is completely free,” said Ly, adding that the festival will also feature a live animal show with a trained handler displaying turtles, rabbits, insects, and reptiles including a large albino python. “The animals are all very docile, the kids get to pet them if they want, and it’s always a hit.” “This is our second year back from the pandemic, so the turnout is hard to predict, but usually we have more than 1,000 people,” she continued. “My favorite part is seeing all of the costumes that the parents and children come dressed up in.” “A few years ago we had someone come in a blow-up dinosaur costume that looked like it was eight feet tall but with a real person inside,” Ly added. “That’s the best part. I can’t wait to see the creativity that people will bring this year.”

articles.text: Part 6 in a series School board candidates answered one more question in week six for Piedmont voters. Each candidate was asked to describe the role they intend to perform upon being elected. School Board 3 open seats; 3 candidates. Week 6 Question What do you see as a school board member’s primary role and responsibility? MICHAEL MALIONE, Candidate I see the board’s primary role and responsibility falling into three areas: Support, Governance, and Guidance. Support - Operating a school district such as ours is challenging. Our district leaders (administration and staff) benefit from having access to board members who care, who are knowledgeable and listen well, and who reflect as they navigate tough decisions and make difficult tradeoffs. Governance - The school board also provides oversight of the Superintendent on behalf of our constituents, to ensure that the district continues to deliver excellent educational outcomes for all of our students and is accountable for doing so in a sustainable and fiscally responsible manner. Guidance - Last but certainly not least, the school board serves to maintain the district’s focus on its primary responsibility – providing the best academic experience for all of our kids – by applying current best practices for pedagogy and curriculum and ultimately codifying all of the above in policies and procedures to guide the administration and staff. SUSY STRUBLE, Candidate The roles and responsibilities of school board members are defined in the Board Bylaws (Section 9000) and guided by governance standards (Section 9005) – see Piedmont.k12.ca.us/ about/policies. I encourage anyone interested to read them. According to these guidelines, no single role or responsibility is prioritized above the others. I cite these policies not to avoid the question, but to affirm that those policies are the answer – and that I will uphold them equally, as previous school board members have done. While I believe Section 9000 blurs the distinction between roles and responsibilities (just my opinion as a bit of a policy nerd), the bylaws are clear and well-defined. MAX ROMAN, Candidate No response received.

Dear PUSD Families & Staff: It was wonderful seeing so many of you this weekend at Legally Blonde Jr., a fun production for our middle school students. Thank you to Amy Moorhead for her dedication to musical theater in our district! Thanks also to the Havens Parent Club for inviting me to speak to our Havens parents, including my partner in presentation, a future Havens student. Presentations are always better with our kids. And finally, a very special thank you to the Wildwood staff and families during this time of leadership transition. Ariel Dolowich and I have provided administrative support during the last several weeks, and we have loved every minute of it. Later this week, we are recommending the appointment of an Interim Principal for Wildwood, and we are grateful to the Wildwood community for their support during this time of change. In partnership. Jennifer Hawn, Ed.D. Superintendent • Affinity Mentors - The Power of Words Thank you to Jean Chen Takazawa and our Affinity Mentors for an outstanding program that engaged our middle school students in a lesson on the power of words, including racial slurs, discriminatory comments, and other actions that create harm in our community and prevent our ability to create an environment for students to thrive. I observed our high school affinity mentors facilitate a lesson, and I was impressed by the overall empathy and sophistication of our students, both our high school mentors and our middle school students. Educating our students on the meaning, historical context, and impact of words reinforces knowledge that eliminates the idea that “we just did not know.” When we know more, we can do better. Barry has a website that includes a tool with which you can explore the concept of antipode with your children. Thank you, Barry Fischer! • The Book Fair...is HERE This week is the book fair at all of our elementary sites, and it’s going to be great! Thank you to our librarians and volunteers who hold this wonderful event. What a wonderful event! articles.text: Have you ever seen a dog shake someone’s hand or sit on command? Believe it or not, keepers at Oakland Zoo work with our animals to train them to behave similarly. If you are at the Zoo at the right time, you might see a bear standing up with front paws on the fence, a macaw being asked to put its wing out, or other interesting behaviors from the Zoo animal residents. Our animals are trained to exhibit different behaviors to help us better care for them. For example, a bear standing up with paws on the fence allows Keepers to check their belly and feet for injuries. This helps ensure the animals are happy and healthy in a safer, more frequent, and less stressful manner. Animal Training Game Using a “bridge” signal during training helps animals understand what action is rewarded, reducing confusion. This signal, such as a whistle or clicker, bridges the gap between the desired action and the reward, which is usually a yummy treat. For this game you will “train” another person to act. First, send the person who will be the trainee into another room, so the person guiding them can decide on a task. Once the trainer chooses the action, the trainee re-enters the room, and the people guiding use claps to direct the trainee. The claps are slow at first and then speed up as the person gets closer and closer to the correct action. The clapping acts as your “bridge” guiding the person to the proper action. Keeper Jessie Sayre asks one of Oakland Zoo’s resident brown bears for a “focus behavior” to steady himself during training. Nathaniel Landers is Manager of Teen Outreach at Oakland Zoo. articles.text: On a beautiful summer weekend August 9-11, Piedmont High School’s Class of 1974 celebrated its 50th reunion with various parties, tours and activities. Fifty years after graduation, the class had a wonderful time reflecting on its journeys to “Achieve the Honorable” over the decades. The weekend began with a Friday tour of the current PHS campus, which simply stunned classmates with its world-class STEAM building, the new Alan Harvey Theater, and even a visit to our previous outdoor “quad,” which is now encompassed by the current library. Thanks to current PHS Superintendent Jennifer Hawn for joining us for the tour, and for classmate Ron Mockel for leading the tour. Friday evening found classmates in downtown Oakland at Drakes Dealership beer garden for an informal, no-host pizza party…a great way to start more in-depth visits with one another. The capstone event of the Committee members Jeanine Loughran Odell and David Bowman, with spouses Ted Odell and Gloria Miller Mike and Julie Bartlett’s Piedmont home was the reunion location on Saturday night. articles.text: Big game for Lagios and Highlanders October 17 was a big night for Piedmont’s football team. Playing a rare game on a Thursday, it demolished Irvington 49-7 on the road in what was perhaps the season’s marquee game for the Mission Division of the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont entered at 5-1 and Irvington’s record was 6-0. It was also Irvington’s Homecoming Night. But Piedmont spoiled their party in a dominant blowout. The game was never close. All drama expired long before halftime when Piedmont led 35-0, with 28 points coming in the second quarter. “It was totally a statement win. They thought they could schedule us on their homecoming game to get a league win. We showed them why that was a huge mistake,” said linebacker Brandon Dicke. Piedmont’s defense was a big part of the beating with three interceptions, including 50-yard interception returns for touchdowns in the second quarter by Miguel Long and Dicke. “I saw the QB underthrew it. It was like my interception against Encinal, I knew I had to keep my legs churning,” Long said. Dicke extended Piedmont’s lead to 35-0 with an interception return as time expired in the second quarter. Instead of playing it safe at their own 16 with the clock ticking away, Irvington attempted a long pass, leading to Dicke’s interception. Staff Photos Brandon Dicke follows lead blocker, Xavier Henderson, on a 50-yard interception return for a touchdown. With three games left in the regular season, it was an important win for the Highlanders in a battle between the top two teams in the division. Piedmont’s remaining games are with Washington and Kennedy of Fremont, which are both 2-4. The season-finale is against Newark Memorial, currently at 4-3. “No one is close to us in this league, we realized that last week against Hayward. We’re sitting good right now. We have momentum right now. This was a full, complete game,” Lagios said. Game Recap Irvington started with possession, but committed a turnover on downs after Jordan Alemania made a tackle for loss on a 3rd down, Miguel Long sprints down the sideline on a 50-yard interception return. followed by Tommy Ashton sacking the quarterback on 4th down. PHS then scored on 10 plays on an 11-yard touchdown run by Lagios with 3:43 left in the first quarter. During the drive, PHS converted a 4th-and-12 on a fake punt and had a 21-yard pass to Rehan Mumtaz. On Irvington’s next drive, Xavier Henderson had a forced fumble and recovery at the 50. Henderson wound up scoring on a 14-yard touchdown reception at the end of an 11-play drive with 9:41 left in the second quarter. Then with eight minutes left in the second, Long grabbed his interception at the 50, leading to him sprinting down the sideline for the touchdown after manipulating the opposing team by hesitating toward the inside. Piedmont led 28-0 on a fourplay drive after assuming possession at its own 21 with 1:14 left. On 3rd-and-2, tight end Cash Elmquist took a reception 55 yards to the Irvington 16 with 30 seconds left, followed by Elmquist taking the next pass into the end zone four seconds later. The Vikings then made the costly error of tossing an interception as time expired on its next series, resulting in Dicke’s 50-yard touchdown return—35-0. In the third quarter, Ashton scored on a one-yard punch into the end zone with 8:18 left, while Jack Meyjes scored on a 15-yard touchdown reception with 2:00 minutes remaining. Irvington scored its only touchdown with 7:10 left in the fourth. Final stats: Lagios completed 12-18 passes for 272 yards and three touchdowns, to go along with nine rushing attempts for 39 yards and one touchdown. Ashton had 21 rushing yards and one touchdown. Henderson had four receptions for 85 yards and a touchdown. Elmquist had two receptions for 71 yards and a touchdown. Defensively, interceptions were recorded by Long, Dicke, and Miles Silver. Alemania had two tackles for loss. Ashton and Faisal Malik had one sack. Henderson had two tackles for loss, one fumble recovery, and one forced fumble. NEXT UP Piedmont (6-1 overall, 2-0 league) hosts Washington for a league game this Friday, October 25 at Witter Field at 7:00 p.m.

articles.text: Photo by Jacque Jumper Piedmont celebrated its four seniors on Senior Night on October 17: Alina Shahid (left), Carolina Romanczuk, Abigail Call, and Emma Eisemon. Piedmont’s girls’ tennis team played its final home match of the regular season on Thursday, October 17 at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, shutting out the visiting Castro Valley Trojans 7-0. The Highlanders honored its four seniors on the roster om Senior Day, Carolina Romanczuk, Emma Eisemon, Alina Shahid, and Abigail Call. “We played too well; there weren’t any close matches. The highlight of the day was our senior celebration. We’re going to miss them a lot next year,” coach Jim Landes said. Of the group, Eisemon is a four-year starter in doubles and Romanczuk is a three-year starter in singles. Eisemon played alongside Call’s older sister, Audrey, as a freshman. Piedmont’s win improves their record to 8-9 overall and 3-2 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. To qualify for the Division 2 North Coast Section Team Tournament, schools must achieve a .500 winning percentage on its overall record or league record—making their win over Castro Valley a bit more important. “We need to stay at least even (.500) to qualify for NCS, so we have to keep playing well. We have some good teams ahead,” Landes said. The Highlanders have three away matches remaining on the schedule before the Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament on November 8-9 at Chabot College in Hayward. Before that, they’ll face Alameda today, October 23, Berkeley the following day, and Bishop O’Dowd on October 29. All PHS needs is one win over its last three to achieve an even league record. They last lost to Alameda 5-2 on September 26 and had a heated 4-3 loss to Berkeley on October 3. Piedmont bashed Bishop O’Dowd 6-1 on October 10. Match Recap At singles, Romanczuk beat Castro Valley’s top starter 6-3, 6-1 at the No. 1 spot. Kate Jumper nearly double-bageled her opponent at No. 2 in a 6-0, 6-1 win. Arianna Kortum won her No. 3 match 6-2, 6-1, while Lila Rosen Photo by Sophie Hess Emma Eisemon is in her fourth year as a starter on the tennis team. won 6-3, 6-3 at No. 4. At doubles, Eisemon and Samantha Huynh won their No. 1 match in straight sets, 6-1, 6-3. Seniors Shahid and Call paired at No. 2, winning in straight sets 6-4, 6-1. Ella Thomasson and Chiara Silvia made their varsity debuts at the No. 3 spot, winning 6-4, 6-3. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-9 overall, (3-2 league) travels to Washington Park in Alameda to face the Alameda Hornets today, October 23, at 3:30 p.m. They also travel to the Berkeley Tennis Club to face Berkeley High on Thursday, October 24 at the same time. Their regular-season finale against Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, October 29 will be played at Merritt College. articles.text: Photos by Karen Tsoi Leighton Mand (3193) led the girls’ cross-country team at the Wilder Invitational, finishing 43rd of 188 runners. Piedmont High’s cross country team wrapped up a busy week with a pair of meets. They recently completed its second Western Alameda County Conference meet of the season on Wednesday, October 16, while they took to Hayward High for the Wilder Mariner Invitational hosted by Moreau Catholic on Saturday, October 19. At the WACC meet, Piedmont’s girls’ team placed fourth of nine schools while the boys’ were fifth of nine. At the P. Wilder Invitational, PHS’ girls finished 11th of 26 teams in The Championship division; the boys’ were 12th of 33 in the Varsity Open division. “With so much racing on the calendar this month and with little time to rest in between the meets, the athletes are feeling the fatigue in their legs. Unfortunately, many runners have also been or are currently sick and that’s been tough on their training and racing performances,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. Piedmont has its final league meet of the season today, October 23, before returning to Hayward High for the WACC Championship on Saturday, November 9. “We have another meet on Wednesday and then will have about 15 days without racing to rest up and get ready for the WACC League Championship on November 9th,” Zirkelbach said. Wilder Invitational Sophomore Leighton Mand led the way for the girls’ team, placing 43rd in a field of 188 runners with a time of 19:38.07 on the three-mile course. It eclipsed her previous best three-mile time by 48 seconds. It was also an impressive display from standout freshman Viviane Oesterer, who was 53rd in 19:53.33. “Viviane Oesterer and Leighton Mand both started out conservatively and moved their way up toward the front, completing the three-mile course in under 20 minutes—a first for both of them. Mand notched a 48 second PR and Oesterer a 37 second PR,” Zirkelbach said. Behind them was junior Cora Chun in 69th in 20:18.79, while junior Skylar Best and senior Caroline Taylor finished backto-back in 81st and 82nd with respective times of 20:38.06 and 20:39.67. Sophomore Sebastien Swain had a strong day, leading the boys’ team with a sixth place finish in a field of 244 runners and a time of 16:26.25. “Sebastien Swain showed up to the race feeling a little sick, but was still able to keep up with the competition in the Varsity Open race,” Zirkelbach said. Behind him was junior Noah Sohn finishing 38th in 17:16.16. Sophomore Thomas Ero placed 45th in 17:25.61, junior Devon Thai was 93rd in 18:16.23, while senior Oliver Horsley was 145th in 19:14.07. WACC Meet Oesterer was Piedmont’s lead-runner in 22nd of 71 runners with a time of 20:30.55. From there, PHS’ next five runners finished in order with four qualifying toward the Highlanders’ point total, including sophomore Cora Brozowski Schrader in 25th in 20:33.78, Best in 20:35.51, Mand in 20:35.36, and Amalia Gray in 20:38.40. Taylor also finished 29th in 20:39.27. For the boys’ squad, Sohn led and was 18th overall of 79 runners in 17:10.75. Swain was 22nd in 17:24.01, sophomore Alex Schleuning was behind him in 23rd in 17:25.45, Ero was 42nd in 17:54.29, while Horsley rounded things out in 44th, 17:55. articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont looks ahead to its final match of the season on October 24. Piedmont’s girls’ volleyball team is wrapping up its season after recently suffering three straight losses against Western Alameda County Conference teams. It has one remaining match. The Highlanders lost by scores of 3-0 to Berkeley on October 15, ng Encinal on October 16, and Castro Valley on October 18. “We are low on numbers at this point and teams are attacking our weak points,” coach Mariah Cardenas said. Despite taking the losses, Piedmont had some closely contested sets against all three teams. They went to an extra point in their third-set loss against Berkeley, which finished 26-24. They finished within four of Encinal in the third set, a 25-21 loss, while they finished within six points in all three sets versus Castro Valley, including a close 26-24 loss in the second set. With a team of one junior, six sophomores, and two freshmen, Cardenas knew this would be a rebuilding year. Piedmont has shown glimpses of brilliance, including its 3-0 win over Alameda on October 11, but they are still working on building a fluid attack. With time, the goal is for players to continue molding together in time for 2025 and 2026 campaigns. “I want us to swing and go crazy instead of tipping it and being tentative. You’ll see spurts of greatness where we are getting a hand on the ball, but then we’ll commit and error and get in our own heads a bit,” Cardenas said. 3-0 shutout by Berkeley Piedmont fell by scores of 25-10, 25-18, 26-24. In the first set, PHS’ Jules DeYoung gained two kills while Fiona Olsen and Stella Wilks had one. Olsen added two more in the second set, while Charli Panico had a pair as well. Wilks and Mira Sachs had individual kills in the second set. In the third set, Wilks led the way with four spikes while Olsen had three. DeYoung and Sachs added individual kills. articles.text: After coming off of a tough loss at Hayward the previous week, Piedmont’s Junior Varsity football team looked to bounce back against the Irvington Vikings. They did just that in a dominant 48-6 blowout win over Irvington at Tak Fudenna Stadium in Fremont. The result was similar to the varsity’s 49-7 win. Irvington had the first possession of the game and was immediately forced into a turnover on downs. Although the offense suffered a fumble on its first play, the defense forced a punt. The Highlanders marched down the field on the ensuing drive and capped it off with a 30-yard touchdown reception by Diego Hurwitz. Piedmont’s defense continued to dominate and quickly get the ball back. On its next drive PHS converted a 3rd-and-long situation with a 35-yard screen pass to Jonah Cha-Foster, who reversed field for a big run. After big carries by Noah Hussain and Eric Venner, Cha-Foster took a quarterback keeper into the end zone. Irvington ended its next drive quickly after ta pass was intercepted by Mateo Long, his first of the season, returning the ball to the five-yard line. The Highlanders took advantage on an end-around to Hurwitz for the touchdown. Piedmont’s defense didn’t turn down the heat, recording another interception on Irvington’s next drive, this time with linebacker George Saunders returning the ball to he Irvington’s one-yard line. Quarterback Jimmy Lagios then connected with Xavier Laroche for a touchdown and his first reception of the season. With one minute left in the half, Hussain ran in for a touchdown to make it 35-0, the same halftime score as the varsity. The Highlanders came out of halftime excited to continue their dominance. Hurwitz returned the opening kickoff for a touchdown for his 14th touchdown of the year. Irvington scored its only touchdown late in the third. Cha-Foster came into the game at quarterback in the 4th quarter to end the game and Eric Venner put the cherry on top by rushing for a touchdown for the one-sided 48-6 victory. NEXT UP Piedmont (4-2-1 overall, 1-1 league) hosts Washington for a league game at Witter Field this on Friday, October 25, at 4:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont High played its last flag football game at Witter Field for its regular season on Monday, October 21, falling to 6-2 to Berkeley in a strong defensive showing. The Highlanders honored its eight seniors for Senior Night: Dorothy Nemeth, Miya Fujimoto, Ella Yasar, Mary Schickedanz, Alma Ruberto, Lucy Barton, and Eunice and Cyntiche Kouadio. “The seniors had a good night tonight, which is great to see. It’s going to be hard replacing them because they are the original players,” said coach Beth Black. Piedmont’s only points came on a safety where rusher Elspeth Grippando locked down Berkeley’s running back in her own end zone. “I knew they did a lot of handoffs and it tricked me a few times, but adjusting paid off,” Grippando said of the play. Grippando has been a bright spot this season as a rushing defender on every single play. She’s recording sacks in every game since moving into the role and poses problems for quarterbacks, forcing them into quick decisions. Grippando, who also plays soccer, found the ability to translate her pressing on the pitch into pressure on the gridiron. “I was put on rush and something clicked. I like rushing, I feel like I can change the game there. It’s perfect because I can just chase people. I play soccer and that’s a lot of running,” Grippando said. The result brought their record to 5-10, now suffering their fifth loss in a row. The Highlanders’ offense has scored one touchElspeth Grippando sacks the Berkeley quarterback. Staff Photos Piedmont honored its eight seniors on the flag football roster. Pictured on Senior Day are coach Beth Black (back left), assistant coach Hayley Adams, Ella Yasar, Alma Ruberto, Miya Fujimoto, Cyntiche Kouadio, assistant coach Reggie Smith, Dorothy Nemeth (front left), Mary Schickedanz, Lucy Barton, and Eunice Kouadio. down or less in every game during the span. Black knows their offense needs to get into the end zone to win games. “Our defense is holding people down and once we connect all the pieces, we’re going to be amazing. We need to score touchdowns, that’s really it, that’s what I’m looking for in these last games,” Black said. Piedmont travels to Arroyo in San Lorenzo for its final regular season game on October 23 before the Western Alameda County Conference tournament with the first round next week on Monday, October 28. To qualify for the tournament, PHS must be among the best four teams in the WACC’s North Division. Game Recap Both teams traded possession until Berkeley broke the deadlock with 8:08 left in the first half. Piedmont’s defense forced a Yellowjackets punt in its first possession, including a pass defense from Yasar, while they forced a turnover on downs at its own 23 on Berkeley next drive. Dahlia Osman had a pass defense on Berkeley’s third series, helping toward a punt. Berkeley scored after taking an interception to Piedmont’s 14-yard line, hurling a 14-yard touchdown to the back corner of the end zone. A failed two-point conversion kept the game at 6-0 with 7:25 left in the first half. But Piedmont’s offense just couldn’t find the finishing touch despite putting together long drives. They had a 10-play series stall out at the Berkeley 27 with 15:40 remaining in the game. After forcing a punt thanks to a sack by Grippando, another _-play drive die after getting into the red zone. During the series, Nemeth was found for gains of 12 and 21. However, PHS committed another interception on 3rd-andGoal with 8:30 left. Keeping PHS in the game was Osman grabbing an interception with 4:40 on the clock, taking it to the 33. Piedmont drove down to the Berkeley 3-yard line, but an incomplete pass in the back of the end zone on 4th down caused a turnover on downs. Shortly after, Grippando tackled Berkeley’s running back in the end zone for a safety with 43 seconds left. On 3rd-and-17, Berkeley grabbed another interception. Final stats: Grippando had seven tackles, two sacks and two tackles for loss. Osman had one interception, one pass defense, and four tackles. Nemeth had five receptions. Yasar had three pass defenses. Fujimoto had seven carries and two receptions. articles.text: TheatreWorks’ 54th season is opening with the regional premiere of Pulitzer Prize finalist Rajiv Joseph’s play King James, with performances through Sunday, November 3 in Mountain View. This brilliant buddy comedy brings basketball to the center stage as superfans Matt and Shawn forge a friendship through their shared love of the Cleveland Cavaliers and the team’s star player, LeBron James. Spanning 12 years from James’ rookie season to his NBA championship game, tensions mount both on and off the court for the duo of friends in this honest exploration of love, redemption and the power of a good game to bring people together. King James first premiered Off-Broadway at the Manhattan Theatre Club, in a co-production with Steppenwolf Theatre Company and Center Theatre Group. The New York Times lauded the play as “a touching examination of male friendship and the powerful social currents beneath it.” The San Diego Union-Tribune hailed it as “enormously entertaining. A touching and funny story on the game of life and the audience wins every night.” Giovanna Sardelli directs the production, continuing a long tenure at TheatreWorks where, as its Artistic Director, she has directed Archduke, The Lake Effect, and The North Pool. She also directed Rajiv Joseph’s previous play, the Obie Award-winning Describe the Night, at Atlantic Theatre Company. Tickets ($49-$89) and showtimes for performances are available at theatreworks.org/mainstage/king-james. TheatreWorks is located at 500 Castro Street in Mountain View. articles.text: Award-winning actor and playwright Dan Hoyle’s latest work, Takes All Kinds, closes its first official run at The Marsh in San Francisco this Saturday, October 26. Directed by Aldo Billingslea and Michael Moran and developed with Charlie Varon, the play follows Hoyle as he travels across what he finds to be a polarized United States in an explosive election year. As Hoyle discovers a country full of rage and fear, he also encounters citizens who are joyfully and creatively attempting to unite the country against divisive odds. Continuing his brand of journalistic theater that has been called “riveting, funny and poignant” by The New York Times, Hoyle showcases the front lines of the biggest political battles in the country — including school board showdowns in Florida; organizers in the streets of Atlanta; churches in Charleston, South Carolina; and even a former violent extremist in Missouri who has since deradicalized hundreds of other violent extremists. Dan Hoyle becomes a panoply of different characters in his new solo show, Takes All Kinds, running at The Marsh San Francisco through this Saturday. In Takes All Kinds, audiences will see Hoyle bring to life the moving, funny, raw and surprising true stories of unlikely changemakers in this fresh exploration of America’s conflicting and collective psyche in 2024. Tickets ($20-$35 sliding scale, $50 and $100 reserved) and showtimes for performances at The Marsh (1062 Valencia Street in San Francisco) are available at themarsh.org.

articles.text: Major exhibition through January shows role of “women’s work” “Mary Cassatt at Work,” a major exhibition focused on the great woman Impressionist, is now on view at San Francisco’s Legion of Honor through January 26. The exhibition presents Cassatt (1844–1926), the most celebrated woman artist of her era, as a fiercely professional artist and an aesthetically radical painter and printmaker who helped shape the French Impressionist movement and transform the course of modern art. Cassatt produced images of “women’s work”— knitting, needlepoint, bathing children, and nursing infants — that also testify to the artistic work of the woman who made them. Juxtaposing paintings, pastels and prints, Mary Cassatt at Work explores the artist’s activity across media, revealing the daring methods she used to give form to her ideas. In the first North American retrospective exhibit of Cassatt’s works in 25 years, the Legion of Honor is this exhibition’s sole West Coast venue, featuring approximately 100 works. “‘Mary Cassatt at Work’ disrupts any preconceived notion that Cassatt was a sentimental painter and sheds fresh light on her groundbreaking practice,” said Thomas P. Campbell, director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. The exhibition shows Cassatt’s multifaceted exploration of modern life, particularly focusing on the roles of women and children during the late 19th century. It begins with groundbreaking early Mary Cassatt, “Little Girl in a Blue Armchair,” 1877–1878. The Impressionist painter’s work is now on view through January in a major new exhibit at the Legion of Honor. Impressionist works portraying women in the audience at the Paris Opera. Moving through Cassatt’s career, the exhibition includes depictions of bourgeois women engaged in various tasks, acute portrayals of children and revolutionary color etchings inspired by Japanese woodblock prints. The show delves into Cassatt’s process, challenging conventional notions of finish in both women’s work and artistic work, emphasizing experimentation and revision in her printmaking and painting. “Mary Cassatt at Work” concludes with the artist’s persistent return to the theme of women and children in the “modern Madonnas” of her final decade. Often stereotyped as sentimental, these pictures reveal Cassatt’s ability to extract infinite variation from a single motif of mother and child “In a sense, the mother-andchild theme was to Cassatt’s final decades what water lilies were to Monet’s or apples to Cézanne’s. Because this motif is and was so freighted with gendered meaning, it’s been too easy to write these pictures off as sentimental, when in fact they’re formally rigorous, engaged in an ever-deepening conversation with tradition and an ever-more experimental handling of paint,” said organizing curator Emily A. Beeny. “Given the social realities of Cassatt’s time, it’s perhaps useful to reflect on the fact that these works are all, in some sense, brought to us by Cassatt’s own childless state,” she added. “The ambitions of her career were, alas, often incompatible in the late 19th century with childbearing, even for a woman of her elevated social class.” The Legion of Honor, located in Lincoln Park, 100 34th Avenue in San Francisco, is open 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org, or at the front desk.

articles.text: “We Have a History” – visual artist Leilah Babirye’s first solo U.S. museum exhibition – is closing at the de Young Museum in San Francisco after this Saturday. Born in Kampala, Uganda and based in New York, Babirye transforms natural clay, wood, ceramic and found materials into modern objects that reclaim sculptural and carving traditions from West and Central Africa. With 12 new sculptures exhibited alongside works from the de Young’s historical African Art collection, Babirye illuminates the connections between past and present folk art, and the evolving nature of both Western and African art. Babirye whittles, scorches, and burnishes her wood sculptures and hand-builds her ceramics, firing them with expressive glazes. As a final touch, she adorns these works with wire, bicycle chains, inner tubes, scrap metal and other found materials collected from the streets of New York. Her choice to use discarded materials in her work is an intentional nod to the historical status of gay individuals in Uganda. The pejorative term for the gay community in the Ugandan language of Ganda is “abasiyazi,” meaning “sugarcane husk.” In other words, Babirye has said, “It means rubbish – the part of the sugarcane you throw out.” Babirye reclaims this term for discarded debris as a gesture of liberation in her work. Her sculptures range in scale from towering totemic forms to busts, talismans, and masks that form metal- and nail-adorned portraits of the LGBT community. This portrayed community includes princes and princesses within Buganda’s royal family who flouted homophobic cultural attitudes then and now. One of the largest of the medieval kingdoms in present-day Uganda, Buganda was established in the late 14th century along the shore of Lake Victoria and evolved to become an important and powerful state during the nineteenth century. “Leilah Babirye represents a new generation of sculptors transcending traditional boundaries while maintaining a deep connection to its roots. Her monumental sculptures have become recognized symbols celebrating the resilience and ingenuity of African people while also preserving their rich cultural heritage,” said Natasha Becker, curator of African Art at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Babirye has pushed sculpture forward by creating some of the most interesting, challenging, and ambitious forms—freely transforming the body, prodding social taboos, and redefining beauty,“ added Becker. The de Young Museum, 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park, is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org/events. articles.text: Visual artist Jessica Monette’s first solo exhibition, “Unveiling Histories: A Fabricated Archive,” is now on view at Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco through December 15. The show features mixed-media works that Monette crafted as a vehicle to navigate the profound loss and personal trauma left in the wake of Hurricane Katrina. Her research for the exhibition included DNA testing, collecting oral histories and photographic documentation, examining how the impact of natural ruin is historically accumulated. The New Orleans-born artist’s work is deeply rooted in familial history and heritage. Each work in “Unveiling Histories,” the fourth exhibition in MoAd’s 2024-2025 Emerging Artist Program, is a material expression of recovery from personal harm on the one hand, and a broader critique of marginalization of the social underclasses most vulnerable to disasters like Katrina on the other. Monette joins this program as a Jessica Monette, “Untitled (Decimation),” 2024, is among the works on view in “Unveiling Histories: A Fabricated Archive,” at Museum of the African Diaspora this month through December 15. 2024 Stanford MFA graduate. In her first exhibit since graduating, she uses visual motifs borrowed from aerial surveys of Hurricane Katrina’s impact. Additional materials used include commercial building materials such as house paint, plaster and thin-set mortar. The works’ archival look is amplified by the inclusion of site-specific soils and waters, as well as protective and healing ingredients like brick dust, Agua de Florida and cascarilla. Soil from both Georgia and California represent the physical patterns of forced and voluntary migration in the artist’s family, while water from the Mississippi River and Lake Pontchartrain signals a layered narrative that links past, present and future. Rope used in the works is a symbolic bridge between the weight of a violent past and the preserving ancestral bonds of DNA, expressing what Monette has called “integral fibers that resist erasure.” The Museum of the African Diaspora (685 Mission St., San Francisco) is open 11 a.m. through 6 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday, and 12 p.m. through 5 p.m. on Sundays. The exhibition presents Cassatt (1844–1926), the most celebrated woman artist of her era, as a fiercely professional artist and an aesthetically radical painter and printmaker who helped shape the French Impressionist movement and transform the course of modern art. Cassatt produced images of “women’s work”— knitting, needlepoint, bathing children, and nursing infants — that also testify to the artistic work of the woman who made them. Juxtaposing paintings, pastels and prints, Mary Cassatt at Work explores the artist’s activity across media, revealing the daring methods she used to give form to her ideas. In the first North American retrospective exhibit of Cassatt’s works in 25 years, the Legion of Honor is this exhibition’s sole West Coast venue, featuring approximately 100 works. “‘Mary Cassatt at Work’ disrupts any preconceived notion that Cassatt was a sentimental painter and sheds fresh light on her groundbreaking practice,” said Thomas P. Campbell, director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. The exhibition shows Cassatt’s multifaceted exploration of modern life, particularly focusing on the roles of women and children during the late 19th century. It begins with groundbreaking early Mary Cassatt, “Little Girl in a Blue Armchair,” 1877–1878. The Impressionist painter’s work is now on view through January in a major new exhibit at the Legion of Honor. Impressionist works portraying women in the audience at the Paris Opera. Moving through Cassatt’s career, the exhibition includes depictions of bourgeois women engaged in various tasks, acute portrayals of children and revolutionary color etchings inspired by Japanese woodblock prints. The show delves into Cassatt’s process, challenging conventional notions of finish in both women’s work and artistic work, emphasizing experimentation and revision in her printmaking and painting. “Mary Cassatt at Work” concludes with the artist’s persistent return to the theme of women and children in the “modern Madonnas” of her final decade. Often stereotyped as sentimental, these pictures reveal Cassatt’s ability to extract infinite variation from a single motif of mother and child “In a sense, the mother-andchild theme was to Cassatt’s final decades what water lilies were to Monet’s or apples to Cézanne’s. Because this motif is and was so freighted with gendered meaning, it’s been too easy to write these pictures off as sentimental, when in fact they’re formally rigorous, engaged in an ever-deepening conversation with tradition and an ever-more experimental handling of paint,” said organizing curator Emily A. Beeny. “Given the social realities of Cassatt’s time, it’s perhaps useful to reflect on the fact that these works are all, in some sense, brought to us by Cassatt’s own childless state,” she added. “The ambitions of her career were, alas, often incompatible in the late 19th century with childbearing, even for a woman of her elevated social class.” The Legion of Honor, located in Lincoln Park, 100 34th Avenue in San Francisco, is open 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org, or at the front desk. “Unveiling Histories” exhibit opens at MoAD By Selen Ozturk Visual artist Jessica Monette’s first solo exhibition, “Unveiling Histories: A Fabricated Archive,” is now on view at Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco through December 15. The show features mixed-media works that Monette crafted as a vehicle to navigate the profound loss and personal trauma left in the wake of Hurricane Katrina. Her research for the exhibition included DNA testing, collecting oral histories and photographic documentation, examining how the impact of natural ruin is historically accumulated. The New Orleans-born artist’s work is deeply rooted in familial history and heritage. Each work in “Unveiling Histories,” the fourth exhibition in MoAd’s 2024-2025 Emerging Artist Program, is a material expression of recovery from personal harm on the one hand, and a broader critique of marginalization of the social underclasses most vulnerable to disasters like Katrina on the other. Monette joins this program as a Jessica Monette, “Untitled (Decimation),” 2024, is among the works on view in “Unveiling Histories: A Fabricated Archive,” at Museum of the African Diaspora this month through December 15. 2024 Stanford MFA graduate. In her first exhibit since graduating, she uses visual motifs borrowed from aerial surveys of Hurricane Katrina’s impact. Additional materials used include commercial building materials such as house paint, plaster and thin-set mortar. The works’ archival look is amplified by the inclusion of site-specific soils and waters, as well as protective and healing ingredients like brick dust, Agua de Florida and cascarilla. Soil from both Georgia and California represent the physical patterns of forced and voluntary migration in the artist’s family, while water from the Mississippi River and Lake Pontchartrain signals a layered narrative that links past, present and future. Rope used in the works is a symbolic bridge between the weight of a violent past and the preserving ancestral bonds of DNA, expressing what Monette has called “integral fibers that resist erasure.” The Museum of the African Diaspora (685 Mission St., San Francisco) is open 11 a.m. through 6 p.m. Wednesday through Saturday, and 12 p.m. through 5 p.m. on Sundays. READ IT IN THE POST Ugandan artist exhibit closes at de Young Oct. 26 By Selen Ozturk “We Have a History” – visual artist Leilah Babirye’s first solo U.S. museum exhibition – is closing at the de Young Museum in San Francisco after this Saturday. Born in Kampala, Uganda and based in New York, Babirye transforms natural clay, wood, ceramic and found materials into modern objects that reclaim sculptural and carving traditions from West and Central Africa. With 12 new sculptures exhibited alongside works from the de Young’s historical African Art collection, Babirye illuminates the connections between past and present folk art, and the evolving nature of both Western and African art. Babirye whittles, scorches, and burnishes her wood sculptures and hand-builds her ceramics, firing them with expressive glazes. As a final touch, she adorns these works with wire, bicycle chains, inner tubes, scrap metal and other found materials collected from the streets of New York. Her choice to use discarded materials in her work is an intentional nod to the historical status of gay individuals in Uganda. The pejorative term for the gay community in the Ugandan language of Ganda is “abasiyazi,” meaning “sugarcane husk.” In other words, Babirye has said, “It means rubbish – the part of the sugarcane you throw out.” Babirye reclaims this term for discarded debris as a gesture of liberation in her work. Her sculptures range in scale from towering totemic forms to busts, talismans, and masks that form metal- and nail-adorned portraits of the LGBT community. This portrayed community includes princes and princesses within Buganda’s royal family who flouted homophobic cultural attitudes then and now. One of the largest of the medieval kingdoms in present-day Uganda, Buganda was established in the late 14th century along the shore of Lake Victoria and evolved to become an important and powerful state during the nineteenth century. “Leilah Babirye represents a new generation of sculptors transcending traditional boundaries while maintaining a deep connection to its roots. Her monumental sculptures have become recognized symbols celebrating the resilience and ingenuity of African people while also preserving their rich cultural heritage,” said Natasha Becker, curator of African Art at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Babirye has pushed sculpture forward by creating some of the most interesting, challenging, and ambitious forms—freely transforming the body, prodding social taboos, and redefining beauty,“ added Becker. The de Young Museum, 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive in Golden Gate Park, is open from 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org/events. articles.text: If you check your dates, you might be interested in coming to the new jazz club in Piedmont. When In the Tradition Jazz Trio plays in the Piedmont Center for the Arts, that elegant space becomes a sophisticated jazz nightclub. That’s the way it was on Sunday afternoon and the music was inspiring. Maybe you’d like to hear some secrets about jazz and improvised music. Jazz as a musical form is one of the miracles of multicultural assimilation. It blends African tradition and rhythms with European musical instruments and musical form. Almost all cultures have gotten into the act. The hey-day of jazz started at the end of the 19th century and blossomed, declined for a while, and then blossomed again. Virtually all of the early jazz players had classical music training. To this classical training, they added improvisation and jazz chords. Good jazz should always sound improvised even when it isn’t. That is one of the secrets of this musical idiom. Virtually all jazz players have an idea what they’re going to do in advance. In the Tradition Jazz Trio knows all of these things and what they produce is an inspiration. Perhaps you know them as Bill Jackman and his Trio – Bill Jackman, piano, Michael Jones, string bass, and Albert Brooks drums. Their program on Sunday was a tribute to American composer Jimmy van Heusen. Jackman told me that he prepares at least 20 pieces for his programs. They rehearse but everything sounds improvised as if they’re making the music up on the spot. That’s how jazz should be. Jazz can be many things. Jackman specializes in a mellow form of jazz, but the group can sparkle In the Tradition jazz trio: Bill Jackman, piano, Michael Jones, bass, and Albert Brooks, drums GOOD THROUGH NOVEMBER 2024 GOOD THROUGH NOVEMBER 2024

articles.text: A scene from The Red Turtle The Red Turtle is a breathtaking fable, written and animated by Oscar-winning Dutch filmmaker Michael Dudok de Wit, working in collaboration with Studio Ghibli, the renowned Japanese house of animation co-founded by Hayao Miyazaki and Isao Takahata. Though The Red Turtle has a PG rating and is only 80 minutes long, it is not simply kidfriendly. What gives this film its emotional power is that not a single word is spoken, nor is a single word needed. The silence of the film falls away as the audience, both young and old, is transported into a captivating story that is completely unexpected/ It is a story that gives the illusion of being slight but is instead deeply complex. The film opens with a raging, storm-tossed sea. Abruptly the head of a man appears floating just above the surface, struggling to survive. He spots a capsized lifeboat and clings to it as the wind howls and the water churns. When the sun rises, the sky now clear, the man is lying on a wide sandy beach. He doesn’t stir until a small sand crab crawls up the leg of his pants and bites him. It’s then that he wakes, slowly stands, and looks around. He is alone. All he sees is ocean and a necklace of sand, finally noticing that just beyond the beach is a forest of lush green bamboo that covers the island. articles.text: Part 2 Last week I wrote about the wines of K Vintners and L’Ecole No. 41. If you read that article you can skip the first two paragraphs of this one.) In my 23 years of being a wine journalist I have traveled to many countries and several continents to visit the major wine regions of the world. One region I had missed was the wine growing region of Washington state. I have had many fine wines from Walla Walla and knew their reputation was soaring, but I had yet to visit. articles.text: Lester Isenstadt, born to Abraham and Charlotte Isenstadt, passed away on September 29, 2024, aged 82. He was surrounded by his family, to whom he was devoted. He is survived by his wife of 42 years, Catherine, and his sons Alex and Joseph. Lester grew up in Cambridge, MA. He suffered illness as a child and was determined to become a doctor in order to provide the same deep care and dedication that he received from his own doctors. He attended Boston University and then enrolled at the University of Arkansas Medical School to train to be a psychiatrist. He told colorful stories of the culture shock of being one of the few Jewish people in Little Rock. After medical school he moved to San Francisco for his psychiatric residency, and when that was completed trained as a child and adult psychoanalyst. He found deep purpose in his work and in helping his patients. He became passionate about neuroscience as the field of psychology became increasingly informed by it. He loved to spend his time studying neurobiological literature to better help his patients. He was particularly interested in how people react to mistakes and showing his patients that mistakes are a gift and a gateway to learning. He was devoted to learning, and used to say that a day was wasted if he hadn’t learned something. Even in his final weeks, he continued to study and remained devoted to his patients and their emotional wellbeing. Memorial donations in the name of Lester Isenstadt may be made to the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network.

articles.text: It was a mild day for the Walking on Wednesdays group last Wednesday with 45 walkers with one K-9 best friend on hand for their weekly walk. The group had not gone to Littlewood Drive this year, so it was the morning’s destination. The group walked on Highland, Sheridan, and Lakeview Avenue to Poplar Way, and stopped at Mountain and Bellevue to catch their breath. The walkers noted the small Island Oak that replaced the iconic Sequoia in the traffic circle there. The original tree stood in this intersection for generations. It served as Piedmont’s first holiday tree during the 1920s and 30s. However, the Sequoia was dying and needed to be removed last fall. Park commissioner Jack Fischrup, a regular Wednesday walker, noted that the small traffic island has no source of water, and a gator water bag has been put around the oak’s trunk. It will be supplied with water by the City for two years to help the tree thrive. The group then headed to Dudley Avenue and a climb to the top of the long Littlewood cul de sac. A group photo was taken, and the surprising history of Piedmont’s Silk Farm from a past Piedmont Post article by Gail Lombardi of the Piedmont Historical Society was shared. At the end of the 19th century there were only three types of cloth - cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government thought silk could be produced in America, and funded groups to create experimental silk producing stations. It was believed silk production could provide employment for women, reduce unemployment, and increase family income. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. The society planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are silkworms’ food, and built a twostory, eight-room cocoonery. The locals called it the “Silk Farm.” an additional seven acres were obtained, and about 100 women were employed. During their lives, silkworms consume 50 times their weight in mulberry leaves, which the women harvested, chopped, and fed to the worms in trays four times a day. The worms reached maturity in 35 days and spun their cocoons. The Silk Farm’s cocoons were fumigated to kill the pupa, softened in hot water, unreeled as separate silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 200 to 300 feet long. Several filaments were spun together to form one silk thread. Unfortunately, the Silk Farm didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese workers were only paid six cents a day. In 1895 the farm closed. The walkers descended the Littlewood canyon where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees once were. Sadly, there are no Littlewood mulberry trees today to give witness to the street’s history. Some walkers remembered two years ago they got a surprise invitation to visit the home at the end of Littlewood with a unique yard by its then owners. Albert and Swee Ling Chen are neighbors and recounted that the owners bought the house in 2014 and wanted to build their version of Bali. Walkers visit site of Piedmont’s silk worm factory By Dick Carter It was a mild day for the Walking on Wednesdays group last Wednesday with 45 walkers with one K-9 best friend on hand for their weekly walk. The group had not gone to Littlewood Drive this year, so it was the morning’s destination. The group walked on Highland, Sheridan, and Lakeview Avenue to Poplar Way, and stopped at Mountain and Bellevue to catch their breath. The walkers noted the small Island Oak that replaced the iconic Sequoia in the traffic circle there. The original tree stood in this intersection for generations. It served as Piedmont’s first holiday tree during the 1920s and 30s. However, the Sequoia was dying and needed to be removed last fall. Park commissioner Jack Fischrup, a regular Wednesday walker, noted that the small traffic island has no source of water, and a gator water bag has been put around the oak’s trunk. It will be supplied with water by the City for two years to help the tree thrive. The group then headed to Dudley Avenue and a climb to the top of the long Littlewood cul de sac. A group photo was taken, and the surprising history of Piedmont’s Silk Farm from a past Piedmont Post article by Gail Lombardi of the Piedmont Historical Society was shared. At the end of the 19th century there were only three types of cloth - cotton, wool and silk. The U.S. government thought silk could be produced in America, and funded groups to create experimental silk producing stations. It was believed silk production could provide employment for women, reduce unemployment, and increase family income. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. The society planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are silkworms’ food, and built a twostory, eight-room cocoonery. The locals called it the “Silk Farm.” By 1885 the grove was thriving, an additional seven acres were obtained, and about 100 women were employed. During their lives, silkworms consume 50 times their weight in mulberry leaves, which the women harvested, chopped, and fed to the worms in trays four times a day. The worms reached maturity in 35 days and spun their cocoons. The Silk Farm’s cocoons were fumigated to kill the pupa, softened in hot water, unreeled as separate silken fibers. One cocoon could produce a continuous silk filament 200 to 300 feet long. Several filaments were spun together to form one silk thread. Unfortunately, the Silk Farm didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese workers were only paid six cents a day. In 1895 the farm closed. The walkers descended the Littlewood canyon where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees once were. Sadly, there are no Littlewood mulberry trees today to give witness to the street’s history. Some walkers remembered two years ago they got a surprise invitation to visit the home at the end of Littlewood with a unique yard by its then owners. Albert and Swee Ling Chen are neighbors and recounted that the owners bought the house in 2014 and wanted to build their version of Bali. They transformed the area at the front into a tropical garden with a swimming pool, water slide, and pool house. Jungle sound effects enhanced this imaginary. However, they later realized that maintaining this tropical paradise was very expensive and they sold the house. The walkers also remembered that in front of the home’s large front gate was an original red London telephone booth. However, like the Sequoia and the mulberries, it was gone. He was surrounded by his family, to whom he was devoted. He is survived by his wife of 42 years, Catherine, and his sons Alex and Joseph. Lester grew up in Cambridge, MA. He suffered illness as a child and was determined to become a doctor in order to provide the same deep care and dedication that he received from his own doctors. He attended Boston University and then enrolled at the University of Arkansas Medical School to train to be a psychiatrist. He told colorful stories of the culture shock of being one of the few Jewish people in Little Rock. After medical school he moved to San Francisco for his psychiatric residency, and when that was completed trained as a child and adult psychoanalyst. He found deep purpose in his work and in helping his patients. He became passionate about neuroscience as the field of psychology became increasingly informed by it. He loved to spend his time studying neurobiological literature to better help his patients. He was particularly interested in how people react to mistakes and showing his patients that mistakes are a gift and a gateway to learning. He was devoted to learning, and used to say that a day was wasted if he hadn’t learned something. Even in his final weeks, he continued to study and remained devoted to his patients and their emotional wellbeing. Memorial donations in the name of Lester Isenstadt may be made to the Pancreatic Cancer Action Network. They studied two mutant forms of the worm, known as lin-4 and lin-14, that showed defects in the timing of the activation of genetic programs that control development. In 2000 Ruvk un published the discovery of another microRNA molecule, encoded by a gene called let-7, which is found throughout the animal kingdom. Since then, more than 1,000 microRNA genes have been found in humans. “Ambros and Ruvkun’s seminal discovery in the small worm C. elegans was unexpected, and revealed a new dimension to gene regulation, essential for all complex life forms,” the Nobel citation declared. After Ruvkun matriculated from Piedmont in 1969 he attended the University of California at Berkeley and then earned his PhD at Harvard University before joining Horvitz’s lab at MIT for postdoctoral training. Ruvkun is believed to be the first Piedmont alumni to win a Nobel Prize. Piedmont Real Estate Update October 2024 The House Price Super-Cycle “Housing seems to have a remarkable ability to keep appreciating, whatever the weather.” The Economist, October 2024 In a recent issue of The Economist, the paper outlined three drivers that they believe will ensure that, for decades to come, the housing market will continue on an upward trend. They are: Demographic Shifts Across the globe, the foreign-born population is rising at an annual rate of 4%, the fastest growth on record. Immigration increases the demand for housing, pushing both rents and home prices higher. Research has shown that even a small uptick in the immigration rate can significantly increase average house prices. 1 The Appeal of Urban Living When the pandemic began, many assumed that the rise of remote work would reduce the allure of living in cities. According to The Economist, this has not been the case. They found that, while remote work is more prevalent, 37% of businesses are still located in larger cities. Interestingly, the same share as in 2019. Consequently, urban centers like Oakland, Berkeley, and Walnut Creek retain their appeal due to the availability of jobs, amenities, and social opportunities. The competition for housing in these cities has remained intense, driving prices upward, particularly in desirable neighborhoods where housing supply is limited. 1 “The use price-supercyle is just getting going” October 1, 2024, The Economist 2 Study by CSU Sacramento and the Sacramento Regional Research Institute Infrastructure and Housing Supply Constraints Infrastructure challenges, limited land, and regulatory constraints have limited housing supply growth. The lack of supply is most notable in cities where restrictions against building new housing are the strictest. Further, recent studies have found that areas with rent-control actually see a decrease in the supply of rental housing. They found that, for instance, rental housing supply in Berkeley decreased 7.5% after two decades of rent control.
